attack_mechanism: `openMSP430.cpu_halt_cmd` lies on this debug-control route into the PC-update logic; the transfer is guarded in the RTL by `openMSP430.frontend_0.pc_sw_wr`. The relevant dataflow is `openMSP430.cpu_halt_cmd -> openMSP430.frontend_0.cpu_halt_req -> openMSP430.frontend_0.fetch -> openMSP430.frontend_0.pc_nxt -> openMSP430.frontend_0.pc`. The frontend admits a halt only through `cpu_halt_req`/`cpu_halt_st`, which changes fetch and instruction-state progression around a safe boundary. Forcing `openMSP430.cpu_halt_cmd` while halt or resume is being synchronized can create an extra fetch, suppress the expected fetch, or resume with stale PC-selection state. The architectural PC can advance, repeat, or resume at a location inconsistent with the requested debug transition.

`openMSP430.dbg_reg_wr` participates in forming or qualifying that software-PC path; the transfer is guarded in the RTL by `openMSP430.execution_unit_0.register_file_0.pc_sw_wr`. During a CALL, jump, or instruction that writes R0, `pc_sw_wr` has priority in the `pc_nxt` multiplexer and selects `pc_sw`. The corrupted target is captured in `pc`, redirecting control flow, skipping intended instructions, or executing an unintended basic block.
